extra.message: Hardcoded Weak JWT Signing Secret — Attacker forges valid JWTs for any username, bypassing authentication on /fetch/customer and /search [verified: `app.config['SECRET_KEY_HMAC']` is hardcoded as `'secret'` (line 25) and used as the HS256 signing key for all JWTs; an attacker can trivially brute-force or guess this value and forge valid signed JWTs for any username, bypassing authentication on all `verify_jwt`-protected endpoints (`/fetch/customer`, `/search`).]

JWT Authentication Bypass via verify=False — Complete authentication bypass on /get/<cust_id>; attacker can impersonate any user and access all customer records including PII and CCNs [verified: `insecure_verify()` calls `jwt.decode(token, verify=False)` which completely disables signature and claims validation; the `/get/<cust_id>` route uses this function, so any attacker-crafted JWT — including unsigned tokens — passes authentication and grants access to all customer records.]

Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) in 404 Error Handler — Remote code execution as the application process user [verified: At lines 100-104, `request.url` is directly interpolated into an HTML string via Python `%` formatting before being passed to `render_template_string()` with `dir`, `help`, and `locals` in context — no sanitization exists. A crafted URL like `GET /{{config}}` will execute arbitrary Jinja2 expressions, enabling full RCE.]

SQL Injection in /search Endpoint — Full database read/write, potential OS command execution via SQLite attached databases or UNION-based data exfiltration of all customer PII and CCNs [verified: At line 200 (search_customer), `content['search']` is directly interpolated via `%s` into a raw SQL string and executed with `db.engine.execute()` — no parameterization, escaping, or validation exists. The endpoint requires a valid JWT but that uses the trivially guessable secret `'secret'`.]

Unauthenticated Access to File Upload / Deserialization Endpoints — Unauthenticated RCE via yaml.load() or XXE file read; no valid JWT required [verified: Both `/xxe_uploader` and `/yaml_hammer` routes accept file uploads with no authentication check before processing (no token verification at lines 221-255), meaning any anonymous attacker can upload malicious YAML or DOCX files and trigger RCE via `yaml.load()` or XXE file read without any credentials.]

Insecure Deserialization / RCE via yaml.load() — Remote code execution as the application process user [verified: `yaml_hammer()` at line 253 calls `yaml.load(y)` with no `Loader` argument, defaulting to the full unsafe loader that can deserialize arbitrary Python objects; there is no authentication on this endpoint, and an uploaded YAML file with `!!python/object/apply:os.system` executes arbitrary OS commands.]

Plaintext Password Storage for Admin and Plaintext Comparison at Login — Admin credentials (admin/admin123) stored as plaintext in DB; any DB read yields immediate account takeover [verified: The admin User record is seeded with `user.password = 'admin123'` in plaintext (line 62), while `/login` compares the submitted password directly against the stored value via `filter_by(username=username, password=password)` — meaning the admin account is accessible with plaintext `admin123` and any DB read reveals the credential immediately.]

Weak Password Hashing (Unsalted MD5) — Offline cracking of all user passwords after any database exposure [verified: At line 119, `hashlib.md5(password).hexdigest()` is used with no salt or iterations; MD5 is a broken fast hash, and any database exposure allows near-instant cracking of all user passwords via rainbow tables or GPU attacks.]

Plaintext Credentials Logged at Login — Full plaintext username and password for every login attempt written to application logs, enabling credential harvesting by anyone with log access. [verified: Line 141 (`print(content)`) dumps the entire raw JSON request body — including plaintext `username` and `password` fields — to stdout unconditionally before any authentication check. Every login attempt's credentials are written to application logs, enabling credential harvesting by anyone with log access.]

Login Endpoint Does Not Hash Password Before Comparison — Registered Users Cannot Login — All users registered via /register/user are permanently unable to authenticate; only the hardcoded admin account (with trivially guessable credentials) can log in, effectively concentrating all access into a single weak credential. [verified: Line 123 stores passwords as MD5 (`hashlib.md5(password).hexdigest()`) but line 143 queries `User.query.filter_by(username=username, password=password)` comparing the raw plaintext input against the stored MD5 hash — these will never match for registered users. Only the hardcoded admin (line 58, stored as plaintext `admin123`) can authenticate, concentrating all valid access into a single triviall]

Plaintext Credit Card Numbers Stored and Exposed in API Responses — Full CCN exposure to any authenticated user via IDOR or normal API use; PCI-DSS violation [verified: The `ccn` field is stored in plaintext in the SQLite DB (Customer model, line 46) and returned unmasked in API responses at lines 168 and 183 (`cc_num: customer_record.ccn`); combined with the IDOR vulnerability, any authenticated user can exfiltrate all plaintext credit card numbers.]

Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) on Customer Lookup — Any authenticated user can read all other customers' PII (name, email, username) and plaintext credit card numbers by brute-forcing IDs [verified: Both `/fetch/customer` (line 163) and `/get/<cust_id>` (line 178) look up customers by caller-supplied IDs with no ownership or authorization check — any authenticated user (or unauthenticated user via forged JWT on `/get/`) can retrieve any customer's PII and plaintext CCN by iterating numeric IDs.]

Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) in /search Error Handler — Remote code execution as the application process user, reachable via SQL error messages containing Jinja2 payloads [verified: In the `/search` except block (lines 208-215), `str(e)` is interpolated via `%` into an HTML template and passed to `render_template_string()` with `dir/help/locals` in context. A SQL error containing Jinja2 syntax (e.g., via a crafted injection payload) would be template-rendered, yielding SSTI — though the exception message content is SQLite-generated, an attacker can influence the query structu]

XML External Entity Injection (XXE) via .docx Upload — Arbitrary local file read (e.g., /etc/passwd, application secrets), potential SSRF to internal services [verified: The `xxe_uploader` route passes attacker-supplied `.docx` file content to `python-docx Document()` which uses lxml internally; lxml's default parser resolves external entities, and the endpoint has no authentication, allowing unauthenticated XXE to read arbitrary local files.]

No Rate Limiting / Brute-Force Protection on Login — Unlimited credential brute-force against all user accounts [verified: The `/login` endpoint (lines 137-159) has no rate limiting, account lockout, or brute-force protection of any kind, allowing unlimited credential stuffing or brute-force attempts; this is particularly impactful given the hardcoded `admin/admin123` credentials and MD5-hashed passwords.]

JWT Decoded Payload Logged to Stdout — Attacker or insider with log access can harvest JWT claim data (usernames, issued-at, expiry) from logs. [verified: Line 81 calls `print("JWT Token from API: {0}".format(decoded))` which writes the fully decoded JWT payload (including username, iss, iat, exp claims) to stdout on every authenticated request. There is no conditional or log-level guard, so any access to application logs exposes JWT claim data for every authenticated user.]

Unauthenticated Registration Endpoints Allow Account/Data Flooding — Database/disk exhaustion; creation of large numbers of attacker-controlled accounts [verified: The `/register/user` and `/register/customer` endpoints (lines 116-131) have no rate limiting, authentication, or CAPTCHA, allowing unlimited account/record creation that could exhaust disk space for the SQLite database — a real but low-severity DoS concern for this intentionally vulnerable test application.]

User Enumeration via Login Response — Attacker enumerates valid usernames to focus brute-force attacks [verified: The `/login` endpoint returns `{'Error': 'No User here...'}` for both invalid username and wrong password (line 154), which does not differentiate between the two cases; however, the `/register/user` endpoint likely reveals duplicate usernames on registration, enabling enumeration — the direct login response alone is the same for both cases, limiting but not eliminating the enumeration surface.]

Missing Null Check Before Attribute Access in /fetch/customer — Authenticated attacker can enumerate non-existent customer IDs to trigger 500 errors; stack traces may disclose internal application structure. [verified: Lines 184–188 access `customer_record.id`, `.first_name`, etc. to build `customer_dict` before the `if customer_record:` check at line 189, meaning a non-existent ID causes an unhandled `AttributeError` (NoneType) crash resulting in an unhandled 500 error.
